Abstract—Few studies apply digital games to grow awareness
about mental disorders, such as depression and social isolation.
In this work, aiming to increase mental health awareness and
focusing on self-care as a form of prevention, we present COEXI ST, a short, interactive story decision-making game experience
for mental health. The narrative is about a socially isolated
person at home suffering from depression, built from the personal
experiences of undergraduate students during the pandemic.
Most of them expressed severe levels of depression and anxiety
due to restricted social interactions. As the game unfolds, the
player can learn more about depression, the character’s thoughts
and feelings, and the story’s context. Decisions have weight; thus,
players must carefully weigh the consequences of their choices.
Index Terms—mental health, awareness, interactive story,
decision-making, game
I. INTRODUCTION
There is no health without mental health which is considered
a critical component of public health [1]. Mental illness
affects individuals worldwide and is defined as a medical
condition that disrupts individuals’ feelings, mood, and thinki ng, reducing their cognitive capacity to relate to others and
participate in daily life activities [2]. Many important factors
(personal, social, environmental, etc.) determine the mental
health quality [3], [4]. These factors are generally associated
with each person’s ability to deal with thoughts and feelings,
the management of life, and emotional resilience. It is also
related to physical health, self-esteem, and managing conflict
and learning [1].
Currently, approximately 280 million people in the world
have depression [5]. It may become a serious health condition
and, at its worst, depression can lead to suicide. Thus, one
of the primary health challenges of the twenty-first century is
the promotion, prevention, and treatment programs for mental
disorders [6], growing awareness about this illness.

Studies have shown that lifestyle can have a positive effect
on symptoms of depression [6], [7], anxiety [8], life satisfactio n [9], and self-perceived mental health [10], [11]. However,
lifestyle choices are fundamentally a complex decision-making
process related to many biological, social, and emotional
variables [12]. Thus, identifying healthy lifestyle choices that
promote psychological well-being and reduce mental problems
is helpful to prevent mental disorders.
More than ever, games play an essential role in combating
and promoting mental health awareness. As an ally, games
have a unique potential to immerse the player in a story,
as a mediator of decision making. Moreover, there is an
infinite and untapped potential for interactive stories that we
can tell digitally. In addition, games can convey emotions
and experiences that we would never imagine going through.
Thus, presenting mental health issues that people experience
in games offers two valuable opportunities: to show people
who suffer from this problem that they are not alone, and
to share with people who do not suffer from this problem, a
short experience of what it would be like to look at life, from
the perspective of someone who suffers from depression, in
this way, collaborating with the promotion of mental health
and empathy. However, few studies apply digital games to
grow awareness, treat or prevent mental disorders, such as
depression, anxiety, and social isolation [13]. We believe it
is vital to address this complex issue, as there is still a lot
of prejudice regarding mental health. Most people who feel
depressed or suffer from another psychiatric condition are
afraid to share their frustrations and anxieties due to the stigma
associated with society.
Seeking ways to spread awareness about mental disorders
and facing the depression subject without taboo by focusing
on self-care as a form of prevention, we present COEXIST, a
short, interactive story decision-making game experience for
mental health. The interactive role-playing narrative is about
a person who is socially isolated at home, suffering from

depression. Metaphorically, we designed depression as a dark
character that coexists with the protagonist, negatively interferi ng with all the daily decision-making moments. The game’s
narrative presents a mental selection of actions that the player
must act out based on personal choices. During the game, the
ability to make choices is indispensable, avoiding doing them
automatically since they have impactful consequences in the
protagonist’s life.
II. RELATED WORK
This section presents the most relevant games in the mental
health area related to this work and a brief literature review
on related scientific works.
Researchers are finding that games can change us for the
better and improve both our bodies and mind. We share the
same view as Kelly et al. [14] that while existing theoreti cal frameworks describe features of both games and health
interventions, there has been still limited systematic investi gation into how disciplinary and interdisciplinary stakeholders
understand design features to help design features in games
for health, particularly those games that touch on sensitive
themes such as depression. In this context, Wehbe et al. [15]
presented a study demonstrating how to synthesize gained in sights from multiple expert perspectives and created actionable
guidelines to design serious games targeting sensitive topics.
In addition, Tuijnman et al. reported a collaboration process
between game designers and mental health experts to improve
engagement through the combination of evidence-based psy chological treatment techniques, leading to the ScrollQuest
game [16]. Also, Hamid et al. designed an application with
contextualised storylines to help students learn psychological
concepts and better identify the negative patterns in their
thoughts [17]. In the present study, we argue that students who
have experienced depression can be more involved in game
design and development than is currently typical. Furthermore,
we took an initial step in that direction, taking the userc entred design paradigm as a starting point, considering the
students’ views about feeling depressed a significant source of
information throughout the design process of COEXIST.
Focusing on mental health, the following games break
taboos by depicting complex topics such as depression, anxiety
and stress in a realistic and well-grounded way, many of
them with poetic narratives and refined art, some of them
bringing emotions through visual and sound art. For example,
Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice [18] has enriched visuals and
was created in collaboration with neuroscientists and people
who experience psychosis, pulling the player deep into the
protagonist’s mind, a warrior named Senua, who shows signs
of mental disorders, hearing voices and having delusions.
At times, these voices whisper tips on how to proceed. At
other times, they manifest negatively, generating tension and
doubt about which decision to make, suggesting to jump
from one platform to another, with the possibility of falling
or even dying. Actual Sunlight [19] presents an intense and
heartbreaking story that challenges the player to confront the
life of Evan Winter: An overweight, lonely, and severely
depressed young professional. At all times, it is like he is
warning the player indirectly that there is nothing the player
can do to help. In addition, dark and moody original music sets
a proper tone for the brutal indifference of real life. GRIS [20]
is a 2D platform and exploration short game with beautiful art
that features simple gameplay. It portrays a process of struggle
and reconstruction of a girl named Gris, who plunges into an
abyss of pain, suffering right at the beginning of the game.
As the story unfolds, Gris grows emotionally and sees the
world differently, revealing new directions to explore. It gains
colour, symbolically representing the progressive overcoming
of obstacles in life. Limbo [21] is a 2D platform survival game.
Although it brings an unusual and somewhat dark setting since
the environment contains many bodies of dead people, it has
beautiful and simple visuals produced in black, white, and
grey. Only seldomly the player has to quickly navigate through
a series of jumps, some of which are unforgiving, leading to
some undeserved deaths of the protagonist. Sea of Solitude
[22] is a thought-provoking game that reveals the themes of
depression, loneliness, and hopelessness, how we unwittingly
push people away and how our actions can negatively affect
others. It is a third-person action-adventure 3D game where
a young woman is trapped in a flooded city, lost on a small
boat. Confused about her whereabouts and identity, she slowly
pieces her life back together. As her journey evolves, water
levels rise and fall to reflect her state of mind, transforming
the flooded city landscape into new areas for the player to
explore with new challenges to face. Actions are not the
strong point, but the representation of mental demons and the
message, that people are not alone in the world. Celeste [23] is
a platform game where the player assumes the role of Celeste,
whose mission is to climb a mountain and face her demons,
overcoming challenges. Another character named Badeline is
very influential and represents the physical embodiment of
Madeline’s anxiety and depression. Their relationship is an
exciting aspect because it means the relationship between
herself and her mental illnesses. Madeline learns that she can
not get rid of her mental health issues during climbing the
mountain since they are powerful. Instead, she learns how to
understand these issues. Journey [24] is an adventure game.
The player embodies a traveller, with the chance to connect
with companions along the way. The protagonist is alone in a
deserted place exploring the secrets of a forgotten civilization.
The player needs to keep an eye out, as there are creatures
along the way that are not easy to distinguish whether they are
challenges to overcome or friends. Journey relates to who we
are and what we are, an experience complemented by simple
but effective gameplay. The game Depression Quest [25] is
not meant to be a fun or lighthearted experience. Instead, it is
an interactive fiction where the player is someone living with
depression, trying to get through everyday life. The player
must attempt to manage mental illness, relationships, the job,
and possible treatments. It has no elaborate graphics and only
presents texts with photos that illustrate an event, followed by
a quest for the player to choose an option. However, the worse
the character’s state of mind gets, the more options are crossed

out until only the least productive and most self-destructive
options are available. Similarly, if the feeling of depression
gets worse, the music will change from melancholy to an
indistinguishable noise, adapting to the character’s mental
state. At this point, the game conveys the message that, as
depression evolves, it can block banal actions that would be
simple to perform by those who do not suffer from this illness.
As a final discussion, we compare the proposed COEXIST
game with most of the previously mentioned ones. The De pression Quest game presents a question & answer system to
the player for scoring or losing points, influencing the level of
the character’s depression. Similarly, COEXIST shows a set
of daily life choices for the decision-making process of the
player. These everyday life choices include positive and nega tive actions and reminiscences, directly influencing the mental
health state of the protagonist and how the game ends. We also
identify a slight similarity of our game with Hellblade: Senua’s
Sacrifice, regarding the fact that the protagonist also hears
voices whispering to influence some of the decision-making
negatively. GRIS resembles COEXIST in addressing that the
more the player struggles to do daily routine activities (instead
of denying them), the more this action is beneficial to health.
For example, at the end of the game, when the protagonist of
COEXIST opens the home’s door to the garden, depression is
under control to the point of having a pleasant experience in
a blooming and lively garden. As well as in GRIS, the game
environment (i.e., the garden) gains colours as the character
manages to overcome personal mental health challenges. On
the other hand, Limbo resembles COEXIST for the constant
battle between the protagonist and himself/herself, leaving
the subtle message that the strength to do not give up and,
thus, move forward and overcome fears is within each one.
COEXIST also has some common points with Actual Sunlight,
for example, when the person is struggling to get out of a
situation inside the own mind. However, the person does not
have the energy or desire to do so, as depression is dominant
at times. In COEXIST, there is no explicit predetermined
objective for the player, as in Journey, leaving the player free
to explore the environment and perform (or not) activities.
As in Celeste, a dark character metaphorically representing
depression surrounds the player: in the former, it is named
Badeline and, in the latter, Mr Shadow. Finally, in Sea of Soli tude there are dark characters modelled as shadows, while in
COEXIST, although not visually represented as a shadow, Mr
Shadow, a dark 3D character who is part of the protagonist’s
life, follows the main character as an actual shadow does. In
both games, these dark characters in most situations discourage
the protagonist from proceeding and managing daily activities.
III. GAME OVERVIEW
This section presents the main artistic, narrative and tech nical aspects of the COEXIST game, including its plot, art
& design, mechanics, gameplay, animations and development
tools.
A. Story and Narrative
This project was led by an educator who is a mother of
two, a game designer and a developer with more than twenty
years of experience. It involved a team of students who enjoy
playing and developing digital games, including many who
have been suffering from mental health issues. On the way
back after the lockdown, the inspiration came from observing
how slowly and fearful people were reconnecting with others.
Most students felt left behind and lonelier than ever. Thus,
from this observation, the game designer empathized with
these people and created the narrative structure that powers the
game, shaped by the experiences of those students who natu rally were open to sharing their feelings about how impossible
it is to face life activities when living with depression. They
helped to understand their life perspectives better and provided
honest and unfettered feedback about mental health. We did
QA testing, a more technical walk through the game to verify
how the software behaved when used, and playtesting during
development by observing players (some of the students)
reactions to refine game design ideas.
COEXIST was designed to grow awareness about this
complex subject that has become after the pandemic more
important than ever. The game story was based on the per sonal experiences of 25 undergraduate students in Computer
Science from Universidade de Fortaleza, in Brazil, during the
pandemic, of which 19 expressed severe levels of depression
and anxiety due to restricted social interactions. Of these,
15 were referred to psychologists and psychiatrists. Every
individual perceived social isolation during the pandemic
lockdowns unanimously: life was stagnant and full of fears
and uncertainties.
The game’s protagonist is a 3D humanoid coloured in ice
white who suffers from depression. In addition, a humanoid
clone of the protagonist coloured in black and named Mr
Shadow represents depression materialized in the real world,
making the protagonist feel sad and miserable most of the time
and persistently with low mood (Fig. 1). Mr Shadow coexists
with the protagonist and follows him/her throughout the day.
Fig. 1. Main character of the COEXIST game and Mr Shadow, metaphorically
representing his/her mental state of depression.
Mr Shadow lives in a metal box next to the bed on top of
the nightstand. It has tiny dimensions inside the box when
Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidade de Fortaleza. Downloaded on January 31,2023 at 18:31:59 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. 


the depressive mental state of the protagonist is relatively
under control. However, Mr Shadow frequently comes out
of the box when the character feels alone, indecisive, guilty,
worthless, with diminished ability to think and concentrate
and recurrent negative thoughts. Every time this happens,
Mr Shadow follows the main character, stays on his/her trail
and never disappears entirely. However, it changes its size:
Mr Shadow gets smaller when the protagonist has positive
thoughts and bigger when depression negatively influences
the protagonist’s behaviour and feelings. Most of the time,
the main character prefers to stay isolated at home and tries
to find motivation and strength to improve self-esteem by
interacting with the surrounding environment, not letting Mr
Shadow interfere with his/her life choices and actions.
In addition, both the environment and the soundtrack change
according to the protagonist’s decision-making. The atmo sphere gets darker as the depression rises, and the musical
theme becomes sadder and heavier. The opposite happens
when the depression level decreases: the visuals become
clearer and the soundtrack more lively. Since this work focuses
on promoting mental health awareness, it is worth mentioning
that the students who participated in the game design, similar
to some other games that deal with depression, stressed that
it is also important to illustrate how a person with depression
sometimes sees the world. Moreover, they argued that even
soothing games could trigger negative feelings when players
fail to level up or when players feel like they have let down
their team. Finally, some of the protagonist’s thoughts were
based and adapted from the original text “Trapped in Darkness:
A Personal Narrative on Depression” by Erica Woloszynski
[26], being accommodated in the game’s plot.
B. Style and Audience
COEXIST is a third-person short game based on narratives
and point & click to interact with the scene’s objects and
make decisions. The game takes place in the main character’s
residence, with 3D environments adequately modelled and
customized with objects, including the living room, dining
room, bedroom, bathroom, kitchen and garden at the back of
the house. The game is based on humanoid characters with a
non-realistic look, with simplified geometric meshes.
As for its highlights, one can cite its plot and narrative, the
depressive style used in the art and 3D scenes composition.
In addition, it has comprehensive gameplay that features
3D characters, bringing the player closer to the narrative to
increase interest in the game. COEXIST is a game to gain
emotional control, offering choices that motivate mental health
to seek a more welcoming feel.
The game’s audience is people with a wide age range,
from teenagers to adults, who feel worried, isolated, anxious,
saturated with information and gloomy feelings, running out
of time, or with difficulties enjoying their leisure time and
their families and friends.
C. Storytelling Structure
COEXIST has a story structure framework particularly
suited to a dramatic arc. We designed it to help the player
think through the game story from the perspective of two
separate halves, with a central scene in the middle that acts as
a reflection point with personal decisions that can change the
main character’s life perspective. Thus, as a straightforward
way of organizing our game narrative, we used Freytag’s
Pyramid [27], one of the oldest dramatic structures. Following
Freytag’s Pyramid plot structure, COEXIST story is broken
down into five stages: exposition, rising action, climax, falling
action, and resolution, as shown in Fig. 2.
Fig. 2. Story structure diagram represented by Freytag’s Pyramid.
Exposition: The game story starts with the introduction of the
major fictional elements – the setting, main character and Mr
Shadow, style, 3D environment, etc. In the exposition, we sole
focus on building the 3D environment in which the story’s
conflict happens. The exposition ends with Mr Shadow, the
character disturbing the protagonist’s decision-making, starting
the central conflict of the story: leaving the house and going
to the garden to contemplate the beauty of nature or staying
alone at home, suffering anguished and perceiving the world
as lifeless and depressive.
Rising Action: The rising action explores the story’s conflict
until its climax, when the main character almost gives up life,
laying without energy on the ground, impassive and unre sponsive. Meanwhile, Mr Shadow stands irreducible beside
him/her. Decisions have weight; thus, players must carefully
weigh the consequences of their choices. Some decisions
let Mr Shadow interfere negatively with the protagonist and
further complicate the plot. In the rising action, the player
gains access to critical pieces of backstory. As the conflict
unfolds, the player has the opportunity to learn more about
depression, the characters’ thoughts and feelings, and the
context of the story.
Climax: The story’s conflict peaks and the player learns
more about the characters’ behaviours. For example, when
the protagonist falls on the floor without any energy to cope
Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidade de Fortaleza. Downloaded on January 31,2023 at 18:31:59 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. 


with his/her mental issues, this is an opportunity to reinforce
through the story’s narrative the importance of depression
awareness, promoting an emotional takeaway to the player.
Falling Action: Here, we explore the aftermath of the climax,
focusing on other conflicts that arise as a result. The falling on
the ground action made by the climax action makes irreversible
changes in the protagonist’s life. Blue butterflies are lost while
red ones are earned. Other critical situations of despair will
continue to arise before deciding to open the door to the
garden. Time passes quickly, and the game points will define
the progress of actions and fate of the two characters.
Resolution: The end of the narrative with two possible ac tions for game over: victory over depression or victory of
depression. The story’s resolution also involves tying up the
loose ends of the climax and falling action. Each choice
has impactful consequences. Both possible end scenes allow
the player to experience and think about depression, growing
awareness about this illness.
D. Game Splash Screen
In the game splash screen, there are several options for the
player, including the Configuration one, through which the
player can choose the avatar to play with (male or female).
In addition, the player can configure the game Language
and Audio Volume. Then, by selecting the Start option, the
player activates the game splash screen animation, in which
a butterfly resting on an unhealthy hand will fly out of the
scene. Simultaneously, the sinister hand (visually symbolizing
the depressive disorder of the main character) will return inside
a metal box (Fig. 3), whose lid closes (at least momenta neously, since depression will return, more evidently, during
the gameplay).
E. Gameplay
The game’s flow is based on the daily routine of the
central character, whom Mr Shadow always accompanies,
metaphorically representing the depression that coexists with
the protagonist, as shown in Fig. 4.
The difficulty lies in making decisions (Figs. 4b and d)
to carry out activities capable of making the main charac ter’s mind occupied with more positive thoughts, helping to
“forget”, even if momentarily, mental health issues (Figs.
4a and c). For example, Fig. 4b shows a note kept on the
dashboard from a beloved family member. The protagonist
can get this special note since it always brings back good
memories or can leave it on the dashboard since it means
little to him/her. Fig. 4d shows the protagonist looking for
the prescribed depression medications lost somewhere in the
bathroom. This searching activity means a hard battle for
the protagonist. Whispering, Mr Shadow tries to persuade the
protagonist not to take the antidepressant medications. Fig. 4d
shows two possible protagonist’s choices: “Apparently, I’ve
got only you as my best friend.” or “I hate you. You always
hurt me with your thoughts.” An additional challenge of the
game is controlling the feeling of anxiety so that the player
persists and resists until the end of the game, opting most of

this moment, the protagonist expresses feeling too tired to
do anything, with energy levels declining and symptoms such

as sadness and emptiness. Simple everyday choices, usually
made with little thinking, attention, or information, became
impossible to perform or unattainable. These feelings chain in

There are two possible resolutions for the endgame scenes
of COEXIST, with Mr Shadow standing firm under the top
frame of the open door: (1) The main character opens the door
and goes out into a lifeless garden, feeling the world dark and
heavy, accompanied by moths and Mr Shadow with its size
proportions significantly increased. It metaphorically means
victory of depression (Fig. 6a); or (2) The main character
opens the door and goes out into a lively garden, feeling may
have joy in life, accompanied by butterflies and Mr Shadow,
who has considerably decreased in size (but not disappeared).
It metaphorically means victory of the protagonist over depres sion, coexisting with it in a controlled way through positive
personal decisions (Fig. 6b).
F. Scoring System
The scoring system is based on the butterfly count, displayed
in the game’s interface on the upper left side of the game
home screen. Blue butterflies count good moments and choices
that decrease the protagonist’s level of depression, while red
butterflies count depressive decisions that increase depression
levels. In addition, the colour of the environment also varies
according to the protagonist’s level of depression: it darkens
Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidade de Fortaleza. Downloaded on January 31,2023 at 18:31:59 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. 


(a) Resolution: Victory of depression.
(b) Resolution: Victory over depression.
Fig. 6. End scenes of the COEXIST game.
when the character is not in a good level of mental health
and brightens as he/she progresses positively. In the scoring
system implementation, the narrative invokes the character’s
happy memories (and sometimes sad) by remembering notable
events from the past to allow reflection. In particular, we
recall many more happy memories than sad ones to elicit
positive feelings and enhance the character’s well-being. We
implemented the scoring system assigning a weight value to
each player’s decision. Moreover, there is no tie; when the
game finishes, there will be not the same number of red and
blue butterflies.
Keeping a character who suffers from depression always
choosing to do positive actions during the game is a great
challenge for the player, especially those who suffer from this
illness. If the player chooses not to improve the character’s
mood through positive decisions, the protagonist, unfortu nately, will not have a good experience. On the other hand,
healthy choices for the mind will lead the main character to
improve self-esteem and mental health. Every time Mr Shadow
gets bigger or smaller, the player collects red (loses mental
health points) or blue butterflies (gains mental health points),
respectively.
G. Technical Details for Animation and Control of Characters
We used Unity3D for game development, Mixamo for the
characters’ animations, and Illustrator and Photoshop for the
editing and customization of images and objects in the game
environment. The animations were exported in “fbx” format
to Unity, making it possible to control animated 3D objects.
The main character and the objects that make up the 3D game
environment are freely available at the website Asset Store of
Unity and Sketchfab, respectively.
To control the movement of Mr Shadow’s character, we use
a navigation mesh or navmesh, an abstract data structure to an
agent to find a path in 3D spaces using waypoints, in the Unity
engine. Through this resource, it is possible to define a path
[28], [29] and make Mr Shadow follow a list of references, in
this case, the protagonist’s path. We defined each path by an
interpolation curve formed by a varying number of control
points, ranging from 0 (to represent the idle movement in
which the character is practically static, i.e., only “breathing”)
to 4 (to model more complex trajectories when travelling
through the 3D scenario). We use this navmesh also to prevent
the player and Mr Shadow penetrate through the house’s walls
and move more fluidly.
In addition, we also implemented a decision-making system
on a context-based point & click. It allows the player to trigger
a signal that enables interaction with particular objects (mirror,
sofa, bed, floor, toothbrush, towel, telephone, garbage scattered
in the sink and on the floor, kitchen utensils, notebook, books,
doorknob, postcards, notes, etc.). This point & click logic in
decision-making throughout the game increases the player’s
interaction with the environment, reflecting the player’s score,
that is, the protagonist’s mental health status. The protagonist’s
activities are of an average person’s daily routine. Finally,
we visually represent Mr Shadow’s size through a simple
calculation that involves the difference between the current
number of blue and red butterflies during the game. If the
resulting value is positive, we use it to transform through
scaling the increase of the Mr Shadow’s size and, otherwise,
the decrease. Throughout the game, the player is free to
explore the house environment and its objects, making the
protagonist move wherever he/she wants (whether or not doing
daily activities). In this work, COEXIST was designed for
desktop platforms and therefore supports keyboard and mouse
input controls. Using the left mouse button, the player can
choose between the options of the initial command screen.
Other keys used for event control are “W”, “S” and “D” for
the character to walk and “V” for answering the phone. In
addition, the mouse is used to choose the actions performed
by the protagonist, according to the possibilities offered during
the game’s narrative, through the interactive 3D scenes.
Finally, each movement of the main character is associated
with a specific sound theme and sound effects in MP3 format,
representing a particular mental and emotional state. The
MP3 files used in the game are freely available in Free

IV. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
The past few years have upended people’s lives around
the world. Thus, the more initiatives there will be on mental
health, the more spread awareness about depression, stress,
anxiety, etc. This work presented COEXIST, an interactive
storytelling game to increase mental health awareness based
on the personal depression and anxiety experiences of under graduate students due to restricted social interactions during
the pandemic.
Depression results from negative bias in thinking processes.
Thus, designing this game was not a trivial initiative. Neverthe less, it was possible to construct an initial metaphor to decode
the main ideas of those who manifested interest and were
open to sharing information about their personal experiences
after the lockdown. In particular, the experience of listening
to people who suffer from depression and anxiety to create
the game’s narrative by learning how to be in their shoes,
seeing their inner world through their eyes, was challenging
and heartbreaking.
As a form of entertainment, games can get the attention of a
wide range of players, being pretty popular among undergradu ate students. In addition, games can link people suffering from
mental health issues, and those focused on offering mental
health support and promotion. Moreover, games are playful
ways of raising awareness of mental health, influencing many
people of different ages, and engaging diverse health and nonh ealth professionals.
As future work, we plan to conduct usability testing to
understand how players will engage with COEXIST, with the
ultimate goal of improving user experience and making sure
the design works well and that all assumptions are validated
to promote mental health awareness. To this end, we must first
apply for ethical approval and informed consent for research
involving human beings and sensitive personal data. From
the lessons learned, we aim to extend the narrative branches
and scenario of COEXIST to improve mental health outcomes
using, this time, psychological theories in collaboration with
psychologists and psychiatrists. Finally, this multidisciplinary
team can further advance this complex and challenging but
vital research avenue by building a framework [30] designed to
help create games that change players for the better, bridging
entertainment, empathy [31] and mental health promotion to
create engaging, meaningful games.
